anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve: The smaller, mostly motor front division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It sends the masseteric, deep temporal and lateral pterygoid branches to the chewing muscles, plus the sensory buccal nerve. V3 is the only trigeminal division that carries motor fibres.
anterior-fasciculus-proprius: A thin band of white matter hugging the grey matter of the spinal cord next to the anterior horn. Its short fibres link different spinal segments (propriospinal fibres), so the cord can coordinate trunk and limb movements across levels.
anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery: AICA arises from the basilar artery and supplies the front-underside of the cerebellum and part of the lateral pons, usually giving off the labyrinthine artery to the inner ear. A blockage can cause facial weakness, hearing loss and vertigo on the same side.
anterior-intercavernous-sinus: A small venous channel that joins the two cavernous sinuses in front of the pituitary stalk. Together with the posterior intercavernous sinus it forms a ring (the circular sinus) around the pituitary gland.
anterior-occipital-sulcus: A shallow groove near the junction of the occipital and temporal lobes. Because the lateral surface has no sharp border there, this sulcus and the preoccipital notch are used as landmarks for where the occipital lobe ends.
anterior-spinocerebellar-tract: A pathway that carries unconscious proprioception (muscle and tendon tension in the legs) from the lower cord to the cerebellum. Its fibres cross twice, once in the cord and again in the cerebellum, so each side of the cerebellum ends up reading the same side of the body.
basilar-venous-plexus: A web of veins lying on the clivus, the slope of bone in front of the brainstem. It links the petrosal and cavernous sinuses with the vertebral venous plexus, and because these veins have no valves, blood can flow either way along it.
buccal-nerve: A sensory branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) for the skin and lining of the cheek. A classic trap: the buccinator muscle is moved by the facial nerve, but the feeling in the cheek comes from this trigeminal branch.
cavernous-sinus: A paired, sponge-like venous space beside the pituitary fossa. The internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve pass through it, while CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its wall. Infections of the central face can spread here, and a clot in it causes eye-movement paralysis.
central-canal: The thin, fluid-filled tube running down the middle of the spinal cord, continuous with the fourth ventricle and lined with ependymal cells. In syringomyelia a cavity opens around it and cuts the fibres crossing in front of it, giving a cape-like loss of pain and temperature.
central-canal-2: A second mesh of the central canal, the narrow fluid channel that runs through the spinal cord and the lowest medulla, continuous with the fourth ventricle. In adults it is often partly closed.
chorda-tympani: A branch of the facial nerve that crosses the middle ear, then joins the lingual nerve. It carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands. Middle ear surgery can injure it and leave a metallic taste.
cingulate-sulcus-marginal-part: The back end of the cingulate sulcus, which curves upward to reach the top edge of the hemisphere. On axial MRI it is a handy landmark: the central sulcus lies just in front of it.
circular-sulcus-of-insula: The groove that wraps around the insula, separating it from the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula (the lips that cover it). Opening up the lateral sulcus is how a surgeon reaches the insula.
cochlear-nerve: The hearing half of the vestibulocochlear nerve, carrying signals from the cochlea to the cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction. Tumours of the nearby vestibular portion (vestibular schwannomas) often announce themselves with one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus.
collateral-sulcus: A long groove on the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes, between the fusiform gyrus and the parahippocampal gyrus. It bulges into the lateral ventricle as the collateral eminence, and its depth varies between people.
inferior-alveolar-nerve: A branch of the posterior division of V3 that enters the mandible at the mandibular foramen and supplies the lower teeth. It is the nerve numbed by the dentist's lower jaw block, which also makes the lower lip tingle.
inferior-frontal-sulcus: The groove that separates the middle frontal gyrus from the inferior frontal gyrus. Broca's area sits just below it, in the opercular and triangular parts of the inferior frontal gyrus.
inferior-petrosal-sinus: A venous channel that drains the cavernous sinus into the internal jugular vein through the jugular foramen. Doctors sample blood from it to find out whether excess ACTH is coming from a small pituitary tumour.
inferior-sagittal-sinus: A small venous channel in the lower free edge of the falx cerebri. It runs back to join the great cerebral vein, and together they form the straight sinus.
inferior-salivatory-nucleus: A small brainstem nucleus in the medulla that sends parasympathetic fibres with the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) to the otic ganglion and on to the parotid gland. It is why a sour taste can make you salivate.
inferior-temporal-sulcus: The groove between the middle and inferior temporal gyri on the side of the brain. It is often interrupted, so it appears as several short segments rather than one long line.
interpeduncular-fossa: A pit on the underside of the midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles. The oculomotor nerve (III) emerges here, and its floor is pierced by many small arteries (the posterior perforated substance).
lateral-fasciculus-proprius: A band of short white-matter fibres next to the grey matter on the side of the spinal cord. These propriospinal fibres connect neighbouring spinal levels, helping coordinate movements that span several segments.
lateral-occipitotemporal-gyrus: Also called the fusiform gyrus, it runs along the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes. Part of it is specialised for recognising faces and written words, and damage here can cause prosopagnosia (face blindness).
lateral-reticulospinal-tract: A pathway from the medulla's reticular formation down the side of the spinal cord. It generally calms muscle tone in the extensors and balances the excitatory pontine reticulospinal tract.
lateral-vestibulospinal-tract: Arises from the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters) and runs uncrossed all the way to the lower cord. It boosts tone in the antigravity extensor muscles so you stay upright when your head tilts.
lingual-nerve: A branch of V3 that carries touch, pain and temperature from the front two-thirds of the tongue. Taste fibres of the chorda tympani join it, and it can be injured during lower wisdom tooth removal.
lunate-sulcus: In apes this sulcus marks the front edge of the primary visual cortex. In humans it is small, variable and often absent, because the expanding parietal cortex pushed the visual area toward the back and medial surface.
maxillary-nerve: The middle division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), purely sensory. It leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum and supplies the cheek, upper lip, upper teeth and palate, mostly via its infraorbital branch.
medial-reticulospinal-tract: A pathway from the pontine reticular formation that runs uncrossed down the front of the cord. It excites the extensor muscles of the trunk and limbs, supporting upright posture.
medial-vestibulospinal-tract: A pathway from the medial vestibular nucleus that runs down in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the neck and upper back. It steadies the head, working together with the eye movements that keep the view still.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve: A tiny branch of V2 that supplies the dura mater of the middle cranial fossa. The trigeminal nerve provides most of the pain sensation from the dura, which is one reason it features in headache theories.
mental-nerve: The end of the inferior alveolar nerve, leaving the mandible at the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip. A numb chin that appears with no obvious cause is a recognised warning sign for disease affecting the mandible.
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve: The small motor root of the trigeminal nerve that passes beneath the sensory ganglion to join V3. It supplies the muscles of chewing, and when it is damaged the jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening.
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle: A small branch of the inferior alveolar nerve that leaves just before it enters the mandible. It supplies the mylohyoid and the front belly of digastric, the muscles that lift the floor of the mouth.
occipital-pole: The rear tip of the occipital lobe, where central vision (the macula) is represented. After a posterior cerebral artery stroke the centre of vision is often spared, because the pole also receives blood from the middle cerebral artery.
occipital-sinus: The smallest dural venous sinus, running in the margin of the falx cerebelli toward the confluence of sinuses. It drains blood from the back of the posterior fossa.
occipitotemporal-sulcus-lateral-part: A groove on the underside of the brain that separates the fusiform gyrus from the inferior temporal gyrus. It forms the lateral border of the ventral visual stream's object-recognition region.
olfactory-sulcus: A groove on the underside of the frontal lobe that holds the olfactory bulb and tract, with the gyrus rectus on its inner side. A meningioma growing in this groove can cause loss of smell as its first sign.
ophthalmic-nerve: The top division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), purely sensory, entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. It supplies the forehead, upper eyelid, cornea and nose tip. It carries the sensory half of the blink reflex, and shingles often strikes it.
orbital-gyri-frontomarginal-gyrus-and-su: The folds on the underside of the frontal lobe, resting on the roof of the eye socket. This orbitofrontal cortex weighs up rewards and consequences, and damage to it (as in head injuries) can cause disinhibited, impulsive behaviour.
orbital-sulci-h-shaped-orbital-sulci: The H- or K-shaped grooves that divide the folds of the orbitofrontal cortex. Their exact pattern varies between people and even between a person's two hemispheres.
orbital-sulci-lateral-orbital-sulcus: The outer branch of the orbital sulci, marking the lateral edge of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. Its shape varies from person to person, like a sulcal fingerprint.
orbitofrontal-branches-of-anterior-cereb: Branches of the anterior cerebral artery that supply the inner part of the underside of the frontal lobe, including the gyrus rectus and the olfactory tract and bulb.
paracentral-gyrus-and-sulcus: The lobule on the inner surface of the hemisphere where the motor and sensory strips meet. It represents the foot and leg and helps control the bladder, so an anterior cerebral artery stroke typically paralyses the opposite leg.
paracentral-sulcus: A groove on the inner face of the frontal lobe that marks the front of the paracentral lobule. Knowing it helps you find the leg area of the motor cortex on a medial view.
parietal-branches-of-middle-cerebral-art: Branches of the middle cerebral artery that supply the lateral parietal cortex, including the supramarginal and angular gyri. Strokes here can cause neglect of one side of space (right-sided lesions) or language and calculation problems (left-sided).
peduncle-of-flocculus: A small fibre bundle linking the flocculus of the cerebellum with the vestibular nuclei. It belongs to the vestibulocerebellum, which fine-tunes balance and keeps the eyes steady during head movements.
postcentral-sulcus: The groove behind the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex). It separates that strip of body-touch map from the superior parietal lobule behind it.
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve: The larger, mainly sensory division of V3. It gives the auriculotemporal, lingual and inferior alveolar nerves, plus a small motor branch to the mylohyoid.
posterior-fasciculus-proprius: A thin band of short white-matter fibres beside the grey matter at the back of the spinal cord. These propriospinal fibres link nearby spinal levels, supporting reflexes and coordinated movement.
posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery: PICA branches from the vertebral artery and supplies the underside of the cerebellum and the side of the medulla. Blockage of the vertebral artery or PICA causes the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, with hoarseness and crossed loss of pain sensation.
posterior-intercavernous-sinus: A small venous channel that connects the two cavernous sinuses behind the pituitary stalk. With the anterior intercavernous sinus it completes the circular sinus around the pituitary.
posterior-transverse-collateral-sulcus: The rear continuation of the collateral sulcus on the underside of the occipital lobe. Along with the collateral sulcus it separates the lingual gyrus from the fusiform region.
posterolateral-tract: Also called Lissauer's tract, this thin bundle caps the dorsal horn. Incoming pain and temperature fibres climb or descend one or two segments in it before they enter the grey matter and connect to the next neuron.
precentral-sulcus-inferior-part: The lower part of the groove in front of the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex). It lies above the opercular part of the inferior frontal gyrus, close to Broca's area.
precentral-sulcus-superior-part: The upper part of the groove in front of the primary motor cortex. Where it meets the superior frontal sulcus lies the frontal eye field, which commands voluntary gaze shifts.
precuneus: A hidden fold on the inner surface of the parietal lobe, in front of the occipital lobe. It is a hub of the default mode network, active during daydreaming, mental imagery and remembering your own past, and one of the first areas to slow down in Alzheimer's disease.
rubrospinal-tract: A small tract from the red nucleus that crosses in the midbrain and runs down the side of the cord. In humans it matters mostly for flexion of the arm. Lesions above the red nucleus give decorticate posturing; below it, decerebrate rigidity.
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve: The thick root carrying facial sensation from the trigeminal ganglion into the pons. A small artery pressing on it near the pons is a well-known cause of trigeminal neuralgia, the lightning-like facial pain.
sigmoid-sinus: An S-shaped venous channel running down behind the ear, from the transverse sinus to the jugular bulb. It lies right against the mastoid bone, so a mastoid infection can spread into it and form a clot.
spinal-reticular-process: A fan of grey matter that projects sideways from the neck of the dorsal horn, mainly in the cervical cord, giving the grey matter a netlike look in sections. It is the cord's counterpart of the brainstem reticular formation.
spinotectal-tract: A pathway that carries touch and pain signals from the spinal cord to the superior colliculus in the midbrain. It helps turn the eyes and head toward a sudden stimulus on the body.
straight-sinus: A venous channel running along the join of the falx cerebri and tentorium, formed by the great cerebral vein and the inferior sagittal sinus. It carries deep brain blood back to the confluence of sinuses.
stria-terminalis: A C-shaped bundle running from the amygdala around the thalamus and caudate to the hypothalamus and septal area. It is the main output route of the amygdala for stress and fear responses.
subparietal-sulcus: A groove on the inner surface of the parietal lobe, separating the precuneus above from the posterior cingulate gyrus below.
sulcus-interm-prim-jensen: The intermediate primary sulcus of Jensen, a branch off the intraparietal sulcus. It marks the boundary between the supramarginal and angular gyri.
superior-frontal-sulcus: The groove between the superior and middle frontal gyri. At its meeting with the precentral sulcus lies the frontal eye field, which moves your eyes on purpose.
superior-petrosal-sinus: A small venous channel along the top edge of the petrous temporal bone, draining the cavernous sinus into the transverse-sigmoid junction. The trigeminal nerve root passes beneath it on its way to the pons.
superior-salivatory-nucleus: A brainstem nucleus in the pons that sends parasympathetic signals with the facial nerve to the tear glands and to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands. A lesion of the facial nerve can therefore dry the eye and mouth.
superior-temporal-sulcus: The long, deep groove between the superior and middle temporal gyri, with much of its surface hidden inside. It is active when you watch faces, voices and biological motion, so it is a key node in social perception.
tectospinal-tract: A tract from the superior colliculus that crosses in the midbrain and ends in the cervical cord. It drives quick reflex turns of the head and neck toward a sight or sound.
temporal-branches-of-middle-cerebral-art: Branches of the middle cerebral artery that feed the lateral temporal lobe, including the posterior part involved in understanding speech. A blockage in the left side can produce Wernicke's (fluent, meaningless) aphasia.
temporal-plane: The flat upper surface of the temporal lobe, hidden inside the lateral sulcus. It holds Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex), with the planum polare in front and the planum temporale behind. The planum temporale is usually larger on the left, the language-dominant side.
temporal-pole: The blunt front tip of the temporal lobe. It stores general knowledge about people and things (semantic memory) and is vulnerable in herpes simplex encephalitis and semantic dementia.
transverse-frontopolar-gyrus-and-sulcus: The very front tip of the frontal lobe, the frontopolar cortex (Brodmann area 10). It is involved in planning ahead and juggling several goals, and is relatively larger in humans than in other apes.
transverse-occipital-sulcus: A small groove across the top of the occipital lobe. The cortex around it belongs to the dorsal visual stream, which guides reaching and tells you where things are.
transverse-sinus: A large venous channel running along the back of the skull from the confluence of sinuses to the sigmoid sinus. The right one is usually larger, and the left is often small, which can mimic a clot on imaging.
vestibular-nerve: The balance half of the vestibulocochlear nerve, carrying signals from the semicircular canals and otoliths to the vestibular nuclei. Inflammation of it (vestibular neuritis) causes sudden vertigo and nystagmus with normal hearing.
white-matter-of-spinal-cord: The outer part of the spinal cord, made of ascending and descending tracts grouped into dorsal, lateral and ventral funiculi. Unlike the brain, the white matter wraps around the central grey matter instead of lying beneath the cortex.
wing-of-central-lobule: The sideways extension of the central lobule of the cerebellar vermis into the hemisphere, part of the anterior lobe. This lobe receives leg and trunk proprioception, and alcohol damages it first, producing a wide-based, unsteady gait.
landmark:arcuate-fasciculus: The association bundle that arches around the back of the lateral sulcus, linking the posterior temporal lobe (Wernicke's area) with the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area). Damage to it with both language areas spared classically gives conduction aphasia: fluent speech and good comprehension, but poor repetition.
landmark:superior-longitudinal-fasciculu: A long association bundle in the white matter above the insula, running front to back between the frontal and parietal lobes. It carries the fronto-parietal links for spatial attention and movement planning; the arcuate fasciculus is its deepest, curved part.
landmark:inferior-longitudinal-fasciculu: An association bundle running along the underside of the temporal lobe from the occipital lobe to the temporal pole. It carries the ventral visual stream ('what' pathway) for recognising objects and faces.
landmark:inferior-fronto-occipital-fasci: A long association bundle linking the occipital lobe with the frontal lobe; it passes through the extreme and external capsules beside the insula. It is involved in reading, semantics and visual attention.
landmark:uncinate-fasciculus: A hook-shaped association bundle linking the anterior temporal lobe (and amygdala region) with the orbitofrontal cortex, curving around the stem of the lateral sulcus. It joins the limbic and prefrontal systems for emotion and memory.
landmark:cingulum: The association bundle inside the cingulate gyrus, arching over the corpus callosum from the frontal lobe back and down to the parahippocampal gyrus. It is the main white-matter route of the limbic lobe.
landmark:corona-radiata: The fan of projection fibres between the internal capsule and the cortex, running up and down beside the lateral ventricles. Fibres to and from the whole cortex (motor, sensory, thalamic radiations) pass through it, so a small infarct here, a common lacunar site, can weaken a limb without touching the cortex. Above the ventricles it continues into the centrum semiovale.
landmark:corticospinal-tract: The voluntary motor pathway shown through the brain: from the motor cortex down through the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the cerebral peduncle and the basilar pons to the pyramid of the medulla, where most fibres cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract.
landmark:locus-coeruleus: A small, pigmented nucleus in the upper pons beside the floor of the fourth ventricle. It is the brain's main source of noradrenaline, projecting widely to the cortex, cerebellum and spinal cord for arousal, attention and the stress response.
landmark:dorsal-raphe-nucleus: A midline nucleus in the midbrain and upper pons, just below the cerebral aqueduct. It is the largest source of serotonin for the forebrain, involved in mood, sleep and appetite; many antidepressants act on its signalling.
landmark:median-raphe-nucleus: A midline serotonergic nucleus in the upper pons, in front of the dorsal raphe. It sends serotonin to the hippocampus and septum among other targets.
